parentTitle: The Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer Care
title: Chronic pain and long-term conditions
blurb: Tell chronic primary from chronic secondary pain, assess its impact on the person's life and support the NICE NG193 treatments that help.
question: Ms Morgan, 44, has had widespread pain for 9 months. Her blood tests and scans are normal and she sleeps poorly. She asks for pregabalin because it helped a friend. Which medicine may NICE NG193 consider for her?

teach.h: Chronic primary and chronic secondary pain
teach.body: NICE NG193 defines chronic pain as pain that persists or recurs for more than 3 months. Chronic primary pain has no clear underlying condition, or the pain or its impact is out of proportion to any observable injury or disease (for example fibromyalgia). Chronic secondary pain is caused by an underlying condition that adequately accounts for it (for example osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis). The two can coexist. Plain English: some pain is a symptom of a disease; some pain has become the condition itself.

rows.label: Cause
values: No condition adequately accounts for it

teach.caption: NG193 rec 1.1.20. Both may exist together: use judgement and shared decisions (1.1.21).

items: How pain affects life, and how life affects pain: work, sleep, mood, relationships.
Stressful life events, including past or current physical or emotional trauma.
Substance misuse history; money, housing and other social concerns.
Strengths: what helps, their skills for managing pain, their view of living well.
Their understanding of the cause, and expectations of the future and of treatment.
Acknowledge that living with pain can be distressing.

steps.label: Exercise
steps.sub: Offer supervised group exercise; stay active

steps.label: Psychological
steps.sub: Consider ACT or CBT for pain

teach.caption: NG193 recs 1.2.1–1.2.9. Antidepressants listed: amitriptyline, citalopram, duloxetine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline.

teach.h: Do NOT start these for chronic primary pain
head: Group
Examples
teach.caption: NG193 recs 1.2.4, 1.2.6, 1.2.10 (limited trial exceptions for CRPS).

teach.text: Two classic traps. (1) Paracetamol and NSAIDs feel 'safe', but NICE says do not initiate them for chronic PRIMARY pain; for SECONDARY pain, such as osteoarthritis, the condition's own guideline applies. (2) An antidepressant for chronic primary pain does not mean 'it's all in your head': it may help quality of life, pain, sleep and distress even without depression.

teach.h: Already taking one of these medicines?
teach.body: Review it as a shared decision. Explain the lack of evidence for chronic primary pain. If the person reports benefit at a safe dose with few harms, agree a shared plan to continue safely. If there is little benefit or significant harm, explain the risks and support them to reduce and stop if possible, discussing withdrawal problems. Gabapentin and pregabalin are Schedule 3 controlled drugs: check for a history of misuse and watch for dependence.

teach.h: Scenario: Ms Morgan in the GP practice
teach.body: Ms Morgan, 44, has had widespread pain for 9 months with poor sleep. Her tests are normal. The nurse explores how pain affects her work and sleep, what helps, and a recent bereavement. She explains that normal results do not mean the pain is not real, and that quality of life can improve even if the pain stays. A supervised group exercise programme is offered, CBT for pain is considered, and her GP discusses amitriptyline. Pregabalin is not started, because NICE advises against gabapentinoids for chronic primary pain.

children.sub: A cause may not be found

items: Chronic pain lasts or recurs for more than 3 months; primary and secondary pain can coexist.
Assess how pain affects life and how life affects pain, including strengths and understanding.
Chronic primary pain: supervised group exercise; consider ACT or CBT, acupuncture, or an antidepressant (18+).
Do not initiate paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, gabapentinoids, benzodiazepines and others for chronic primary pain.
Already on them: shared review, continue safely if helpful, or support reducing and stopping.

summary: You can now distinguish chronic primary from chronic secondary pain and carry out a person-centred pain assessment. You can also support the NICE NG193 treatments for chronic primary pain and explain why many common painkillers are not started.

A.q: Which person's pain meets the NICE NG193 definition of chronic pain?
options: Mr Ash, who has had back pain on and off for 4 months
Ms Bell, with wound pain 3 weeks after her surgery
Mr Carr, whose sprained ankle is still sore at 6 weeks
Mrs Dunn, who has had a severe headache since yesterday
A.why: NG193 defines chronic pain as pain that persists or recurs for more than 3 months. Recurring back pain over 4 months meets this.

whyNot.1: Three weeks after surgery is acute postoperative pain.
whyNot.2: Six weeks is under the 3-month threshold.
whyNot.3: A headache since yesterday is acute and needs its own assessment.

A.q: Mr Evans, 70, has knee pain that matches the severe osteoarthritis seen on his X-ray. How should his pain be classified and managed?
options: Chronic primary pain, managed under section 1.2 of the NG193 guideline
Acute pain, managed with short-term analgesia
Chronic secondary pain, managed under the osteoarthritis guideline
Neuropathic pain, managed with a gabapentinoid
A.why: When an underlying condition adequately accounts for the pain, it is chronic secondary pain and is managed in line with the NICE guideline for that condition (NG193 rec 1.1.20).

whyNot.0: Primary pain has no condition that adequately accounts for it; his osteoarthritis does.
whyNot.1: Long-standing osteoarthritis pain is chronic, not acute.
whyNot.3: Nothing suggests nerve pain; the osteoarthritis explains it.

A.q: Which treatment does NICE NG193 advise against for chronic primary pain because there is no evidence of benefit?
options: CBT for pain
Supervised group exercise
Acceptance and commitment therapy
TENS
A.why: NG193 rec 1.2.6: do not offer TENS, ultrasound or interferential therapy for chronic primary pain because there is no evidence of benefit.

whyNot.0: CBT for pain may be considered (rec 1.2.3).

B.q: Ms Morgan, 44, has chronic primary pain. She asks for pregabalin because it helped a friend. Which medicine may NICE NG193 consider for her, after a full discussion of benefits and harms?
options: Pregabalin
Co-codamol 30/500
Amitriptyline
Naproxen
B.why: NG193 rec 1.2.7: consider an antidepressant (amitriptyline, citalopram, duloxetine, fluoxetine, paroxetine or sertraline) for adults with chronic primary pain.

whyNot.0: Gabapentinoids such as pregabalin are not to be initiated for chronic primary pain (rec 1.2.10).
whyNot.1: Opioids and paracetamol, as in co-codamol, are not to be initiated (rec 1.2.10).
whyNot.3: NSAIDs such as naproxen are not to be initiated (rec 1.2.10).

B.q: Mrs Pryce, 58, has chronic primary pain and has taken gabapentin for 2 years. She reports clear benefit at a safe dose and no significant harms. What does NICE NG193 advise?
options: Stop it now, as NICE says it should not be prescribed
Agree a shared plan to continue it safely
Halve the dose this week and stop it next week
Switch it to pregabalin, which works more reliably
B.why: NG193 rec 1.2.11: explain the lack of evidence, and if the person reports benefit at a safe dose with few harms, agree a shared plan for continuing safely.

whyNot.0: NICE says do not INITIATE it; for someone already benefiting, a shared plan to continue safely is agreed.
whyNot.2: Rapid withdrawal is not advised, and she is benefiting.
whyNot.3: Pregabalin is also a gabapentinoid not to be initiated for chronic primary pain.

B.q: Mr Ellis, 52, has chronic primary pain. He says, 'If the pain is never going to go away, what is the point of any of this?' Which response reflects NICE NG193?
options: More scans will usually find the cause in the end
Stronger painkillers should remove it given time
Quality of life can improve even if the pain stays the same
Pain lasting this long is usually psychological rather than physical
B.why: NG193 rec 1.1.15: discuss that pain may not improve, that a cause may not be found, and that there can be improvements in quality of life even if the pain remains unchanged.

whyNot.0: NICE asks staff to discuss that a reason for the pain may not be identified.
whyNot.1: Stronger analgesics such as opioids are not started for chronic primary pain.
whyNot.3: This invalidates his experience; NICE asks for sensitivity and acknowledgement of distress.

C.q: Mrs Fenn, 61, has rheumatoid arthritis that is well controlled. She also has widespread pain and fatigue far out of proportion to her joint disease, causing significant distress. How should her pain be approached?
options: Rheumatoid arthritis excludes a diagnosis of chronic primary pain
Treat all of it as primary pain and stop her arthritis medicines now
Wait until her arthritis is better controlled before planning
Recognise both can coexist and use shared decisions across guidance
C.why: NG193 recs 1.1.7 and 1.1.21: chronic primary pain can coexist with chronic secondary pain; use clinical judgement and shared decisions about NG193 options and the guideline for the underlying condition.

whyNot.0: NICE recognises the two can coexist; pain out of proportion suggests a primary component.
whyNot.1: Her arthritis still needs its own treatment.
whyNot.2: Her arthritis is already well controlled, and delay leaves her distress unaddressed.

C.q: Jordan, 17, has chronic primary pain. The GP is thinking about amitriptyline. What does NICE NG193 advise?
options: Start it now, as it can be considered from the age of 16
Seek specialist advice before using an antidepressant
Offer regular paracetamol instead as a first step
Use gabapentin as the first choice at this age
C.why: NG193 recs 1.2.7–1.2.8: antidepressants may be considered for people aged 18 and over; seek specialist advice if one is being considered for young people aged 16 to 17.

whyNot.0: The antidepressant recommendation is for people aged 18 and over.
whyNot.2: Paracetamol is not to be initiated for chronic primary pain.
whyNot.3: Gabapentinoids are not to be initiated for chronic primary pain.

C.q: A community service plans acupuncture for adults with chronic primary pain. Which course matches NICE NG193?
options: Open-ended weekly sessions in a hospital pain clinic
Two consecutive courses, each of 5 hours, delivered by a pain consultant
A single community course using up to 5 hours of professional time
Daily sessions until the pain score falls below 3
C.why: NG193 rec 1.2.5: consider a single course of acupuncture or dry needling delivered in a community setting by a band 7 (or lower) professional, with no more than 5 hours of healthcare professional time (or equivalent or lower cost).

whyNot.0: NICE recommends a single, time-limited course in the community, not open-ended sessions.
whyNot.1: NICE supports a single course, and at band 7 or equivalent cost, not repeated consultant-led courses.
whyNot.3: NICE sets a fixed limit of professional time, not a pain-score endpoint.

reteach.title: Treat the person living with the pain
reteach.question: If painkillers are not started for chronic primary pain, what does help?

blocks.body: For chronic primary pain the best evidence is for moving more (supervised group exercise), changing how pain is lived with (ACT or CBT for pain), and for some people an antidepressant that can help pain, sleep and distress. The goal is a better life with pain, agreed in a care and support plan built on the person's priorities.

blocks.text: 'Not initiate' is not the same as 'stop now'. People already taking these medicines have a shared review: continue safely if they help, or reduce and stop with support if they don't.

explain.body: Chronic pain persists or recurs for more than 3 months. Primary: no condition adequately accounts for it, or it is out of proportion. Secondary: an underlying condition accounts for it. They can coexist, and an initial diagnosis may change over time.

test.q: Which condition does NICE NG193 give as a type of chronic primary pain?
options: Osteoarthritis
Fibromyalgia
Rheumatoid arthritis
Endometriosis
test.why: NG193 states that fibromyalgia (chronic widespread pain) is a type of chronic primary pain.

whyNot.0: Osteoarthritis pain is chronic secondary pain, managed under its own guideline.
whyNot.2: Rheumatoid arthritis pain is chronic secondary pain.
whyNot.3: Endometriosis pain is chronic secondary pain.

explain.body: Offer a person-centred assessment of what contributes to the pain and how it affects life. Be sensitive when sharing normal results. For a flare-up: offer reassessment, review the care and support plan, investigate new symptoms and discuss what may have contributed.

test.q: Joyce, 61, has chronic primary pain managed with exercise and CBT. She contacts the nurse with a week-long flare-up and no new symptoms. What does NICE NG193 advise?
options: Offer a reassessment and review her care plan
Start a short course of an opioid for the flare
Advise bed rest until the flare-up settles
Arrange urgent imaging to find the cause
test.why: NG193 recs 1.1.22–1.1.23: offer reassessment for a flare-up, review the care and support plan and discuss contributing factors; a cause may not be found.

whyNot.1: Opioids are not initiated for chronic primary pain.
whyNot.2: Staying active is encouraged for chronic primary pain.
whyNot.3: Investigation is for new symptoms; she has none.

explain.body: Offer a supervised group exercise programme and encourage long-term activity. Consider ACT or CBT for pain, delivered by trained professionals. Consider a single limited course of acupuncture. Do not offer biofeedback, TENS, ultrasound or interferential therapy.

test.q: Which psychological therapy does NICE NG193 suggest considering for chronic primary pain?
options: Acceptance and commitment therapy
Biofeedback-assisted relaxation
Hypnotherapy for pain relief
Psychodynamic psychotherapy sessions
test.why: NG193 rec 1.2.3: consider ACT or CBT for pain, delivered by healthcare professionals with appropriate training.

whyNot.1: NG193 rec 1.2.4: do not offer biofeedback for chronic primary pain.
whyNot.2: Hypnotherapy is not among the NG193 recommendations.
whyNot.3: Psychodynamic therapy is not among the NG193 recommendations.

explain.body: Consider an antidepressant for adults (amitriptyline, citalopram, duloxetine, fluoxetine, paroxetine or sertraline). Do not initiate antiepileptics including gabapentinoids, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, ketamine, local anaesthetics, trigger point injections, NSAIDs, opioids or paracetamol.

test.q: Mr Pike, 39, has newly diagnosed chronic primary pain and asks to start regular paracetamol. What does NICE NG193 say?
options: Start it, as it is the safest first step
Start it with ibuprofen for a stronger effect
Start it for 2 weeks to see if it helps
Do not initiate it for chronic primary pain
test.why: NG193 rec 1.2.10 lists paracetamol among the medicines not to initiate for chronic primary pain.

whyNot.0: Paracetamol is on the NG193 'do not initiate' list for chronic primary pain.
whyNot.1: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are also on the 'do not initiate' list.
whyNot.2: A trial is still initiation, which NICE advises against.
